paper.title: scPriorDiff: Bridging Single-Cell Modalities through Biological Network Prior-Guided Latent Diffusion.
paper.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics sequencing enables joint profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility, yet high-quality paired data remain scarce. Cross-modal translation based on generative modeling enables inference of an unmeasured modality from limited paired observations. However, substantial differences between gene expression and chromatin accessibility complicate cross-modal relationship modeling and the effective use of observed-modality information to guide target-modality generation. We propose scPriorDiff, a biological network prior-guided conditional latent diffusion model. scPriorDiff integrates diverse biological networks into a multimodal heterogeneous graph and employs a message-passing graph neural network (GNN) to learn biologically informed modality-specific representations that capture cross-modal and intra-modal relationships. To enable full-graph representation learning, a prior-regularized cross-modal completion module infers target-modality node representations during inference. The GNN-derived source representation conditions diffusion for target-modality generation. Across six paired single-cell multi-omics datasets, scPriorDiff outperformed eight representative methods and showed strong generalization across batches and to unseen cell types. Downstream analyses further demonstrated that the generated profiles preserved cell identities, molecular signatures, and biologically relevant functions. The scPriorDiff software is publicly available at https://github.com/ChrisOliver2345/scPriorDiff and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23408383. Supplementary data are available as a separate file.

also.title: Integrate multi-omics data with biological interaction networks using Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE)
also.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comprehensive molecular profiling of various cancers and other diseases has generated vast amounts of multi-omics data. Each type of -omics data corresponds to one feature space, such as gene expression, miRNA expression, DNA methylation, etc. Integrating multi-omics data can link different layers of molecular feature spaces and is crucial to elucidate molecular pathways underlying various diseases. Machine learning approaches to mining multi-omics data hold great promises in uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features. However, due to the "big p, small n" problem (i.e., small sample sizes with high-dimensional features), training a large-scale generalizable deep learning model with multi-omics data alone is very challenging. RESULTS: We developed a method called Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE) with network constraints that can seamlessly integrate multi-omics data and domain knowledge such as molecular interaction networks. Our method learns feature and patient embeddings simultaneously with deep representation learning. Both feature representations and patient representations are subject to certain constraints specified as regularization terms in the training objective. By incorporating domain knowledge into the training objective, we implicitly introduced a good inductive bias into the machine learning model, which helps improve model generalizability. We performed extensive experiments on the TCGA datasets and demonstrated the power of integrating multi-omics data and biological interaction networks using our proposed method for predicting target clinical variables. CONCLUSIONS: To alleviate the overfitting problem in deep learning on multi-omics data with the "big p, small n" problem, it is helpful to incorporate biological domain knowledge into the model as inductive biases. It is very promising to design machine learning models that facilitate the seamless integration of large-scale multi-omics data and biomedical domain knowledge for uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features and clinical features.

also.title: Deep learning and alignment of spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomes with Tangram
also.abstract: Charting an organs’ biological atlas requires us to spatially resolve the entire single-cell transcriptome, and to relate such cellular features to the anatomical scale. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq (sc/snRNA-seq) can profile cells comprehensively, but lose spatial information. Spatial transcriptomics allows for spatial measurements, but at lower resolution and with limited sensitivity. Targeted in situ technologies solve both issues, but are limited in gene throughput. To overcome these limitations we present Tangram, a method that aligns sc/snRNA-seq data to various forms of spatial data collected from the same region, including MERFISH, STARmap, smFISH, Spatial Transcriptomics (Visium) and histological images. Tangram can map any type of sc/snRNA-seq data, including multimodal data such as those from SHARE-seq, which we used to reveal spatial patterns of chromatin accessibility. We demonstrate Tangram on healthy mouse brain tissue, by reconstructing a genome-wide anatomically integrated spatial map at single-cell resolution of the visual and somatomotor areas.

also.title: scRefine: hierarchical and contrastive learning for biologically faithful single-cell atlas integration and annotation
also.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) studies increasingly encompass diverse tissues, donors, disease contexts, and sequencing platforms, resulting in large-scale datasets characterized by substantial technical heterogeneity and inconsistent cell-type annotations. These datasets offer unprecedented opportunities to resolve fine-grained cellular diversity and identify tissue-specific, developmental, and disease-associated cell states. However, existing integration and annotation approaches often struggle to preserve rare or transcriptionally subtle subpopulations, depend heavily on extensively labelled reference datasets or predefined cell-type taxonomies, and can generate latent representations that obscure biologically meaningful lineage relationships and fine-scale cellular structure. We present scRefine, an annotation-aware contrastive learning framework for integrating heterogeneous single-cell RNA-seq datasets while refining cell identities from partially labelled data. scRefine learns a biologically structured latent space, enabling improved resolution of rare and transcriptionally similar populations. In particular, scRefine better separates rare or biologically distinct populations that exhibit convergent or overlapping translational states than other integration methods. For example, scRefine cleanly separates SPP1+ melanocytic tumor cells from SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), indicating that it preserves lineage-specific biological identity despite shared tumor-associated programs. Beyond cell-state resolution, scRefine also preserves continuous biological structure, as demonstrated by its ability to recapitulate the developmental trajectory of the frontal brain in a manner consistent with the patterns reported in the original study. scRefine also calculates a confidence score by estimating cluster membership using nearest neighbour computations for each cell, which aids in defining cells with ambiguous or mixed transcriptional signatures. Across multi-tissue immune atlases spanning 92 fine-grained classes, scRefine consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, rare population recovery, and generalization to unseen datasets. scRefine also maintains high annotation fidelity even when trained with only 1 to 5% labelled cells, greatly reducing the training effort and increasing the generalizability. scRefine is available as an open-source package and offers a robust foundation for constructing coherent, high resolution cell-type reference atlases across studies and technologies.
